keyVerseText: And of Hushim he begat Abitub, and Elpaal.
rootMeaning: The name אֶלְפַּעַל (ʼElpaʻal) combines two Hebrew elements: אֵל (ʼêl), meaning God or mighty one, and פָּעַל (paʻal), meaning to do or act. Thus, the root meaning of ʼElpaʻal can be understood as "God is maker" or "God is act," emphasizing God's active power and agency. This conveys more than a simple name; it reflects a theological affirmation of God as the one who acts decisively in history and creation.
usageInScripture: The word ʼElpaʻal appears three times in Scripture, exclusively as a proper name referring to an individual of the tribe of Benjamin. The top translations are consistently "of Elpaal" and "and Elpaal," indicating its use in genealogical or narrative contexts. This consistency shows that the term functions primarily as a personal name rather than a descriptive title, though its meaning silently carries the theological weight of God's active role.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ʼElpaʻal as "God is maker" enriches our view of God’s character as one who is not passive but actively involved in the world and in His covenant people. The name reminds believers that God’s power is not static but dynamic, continually working for His purposes. For the Christian faith, this underscores the truth that God’s providence and redemptive work are ongoing realities, inviting trust in His sovereign activity. It also points to Christ as the ultimate expression of God’s active presence among His people.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Chronicles 8:11, the mention of Elpaal in the genealogy—"And of Hushim he begat Abitub, and Elpaal"—places this name within the lineage of Benjamin, grounding the narrative in historical reality. The name ʼElpaʻal here conveys more than ancestry; it silently testifies to the God who acts within the lives and history of His people. This reminds readers that behind every name and generation recorded in Scripture is the active hand of God shaping His covenant community.
